title: Normal, uniform, binomial and Poisson distributions

videos.script: So far every distribution has been data. Twelve orders, four hundred baskets, five hundred order times. {{data}} This lesson is about models. Shapes that a mathematician wrote down once, and that real data falls into again and again. {{models}} Four of them cover a surprising amount of ground. {{four}} The uniform. Every value in a range equally likely, like the moment a courier turns up inside a half-hour window. {{uniform}} The binomial. Count how many of ten deliveries are late, when each has the same chance of being late. {{binomial}} The Poisson. Count how many complaints arrive in a day, when they arrive at random at a steady rate. {{poisson}} And the normal, the bell curve. Bags of rice from a filling machine, each missing the target by a small random amount. {{normal}} Each one turns a question into arithmetic. What is the chance that three or more of tonight's deliveries are late? What share of bags will weigh less than nine hundred and ninety-five grams? {{questions}} And the normal curve brings a tool you will use in every lesson from here on: the z-score, which measures any value in standard deviations from its mean. {{z}}
